unit.title: Plan to undertake a routine task

summary: This unit teaches you to plan a routine fabrication task from start to finish, as a team leader would. You will learn to read and check the job's documents, set out the steps and a welding sequence, work out materials, time and cost, plan the safety of shop and site work, brief the team, monitor progress against the plan, handle changes, and close out the job with an inspection, a completion report and a review.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). A **routine task** is one the shop does often, with a known method: a batch of brackets, a window grill, a gate, a tank stand, a set of shelving racks. Routine does not mean unplanned. Most costly mistakes on routine jobs come from skipping a check because 'we always do it this way'.

At Level 3 you plan the task for a team: you read the job card and drawing, decide the order of work, work out the materials, time and cost, plan the safety, give each person a role, set the quality checks, watch progress, deal with changes, and close the job out properly so that the next plan is better.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and welders and fabricators who lead small jobs in the shop or on site.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Read the job card, drawing, specification and WPS; check the revision; find and settle anything unclear or conflicting before work starts.
Put the steps in a sensible order, plan a welding sequence that limits distortion, and set the checks and hold points.
Make a cut list, allow for saw cuts and waste, work out stock lengths, paint and consumables, and check materials when they arrive.
Estimate the time for each step, add a contingency, schedule the team, book equipment, order early enough, and cost the job.
Break the job into steps, find the hazards, plan the controls and permits, and plan site work: access, power, people nearby, weather.
Give each person a role that fits their skills, name one person in charge, brief the team, and confirm dates with the client.
Check progress against the plan, find the cause of any delay, re-plan without cutting safety or quality, and handle changes in writing.
Inspect and fix, clean up, complete the records and the completion report, get the client's sign-off, and record what to do better next time.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on reading the task, the order of work, quality checks, materials, time and scheduling, resources, safety, site work, people, monitoring, changes, costing and closing out.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms and quick calculations such as a cut list, a diagonal or labour hours) and essays on planning a job from start to finish.

Two **group practicals**: preparing and presenting a full work plan for a fabrication job from a drawing; and planning, making, inspecting and reporting on a welded frame, with a hold point before full welding.

blocks.note: Show your working in every calculation, with units, and check it a second way. A planner who gets the cut list or the hours wrong costs the shop money on every job.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Document
What it tells you
What to check before planning
rows: What is to be made, how many, for whom, and by when
The quantity, due date, job number and any special instructions
Shapes, sizes, tolerances, weld symbols, material and finish
That it is the **latest revision**; the units; the notes; anything missing or unclear
The client's or engineer's requirements: standards, materials, weld sizes, finish, inspection
That it agrees with the drawing; which one governs if they differ
The approved process, filler, settings, joint preparation (such as the root gap), preheat and positions
That it covers your joints, and that you have the consumables and equipment it calls for
The hazards of paints, primers, degreasers and other products
The controls and PPE needed for each product
On bigger or controlled jobs: each check, who makes it, against what, and which are hold points
That your plan includes every check and hold point

ul: **Is the drawing current?** Even for a repeat order 'the same as last month', check that the drawing has not been revised since.

**Do the documents agree?** If the drawing calls for 6 mm fillets and the specification for 8 mm, do not choose one yourself. Ask the engineer or the person responsible, and get the answer **in writing**, for example by a request for information (RFI).

**Can you follow the WPS?** If the WPS calls for E7018 electrodes and the store has only E6013, stop and ask the supervisor before welding. The WPS is the approved method; changing the consumable without approval changes the weld.
**Is anything unclear?** Ask before you start, not after the steel is cut.
**What does 'done' mean?** The finish, the inspection, the delivery or fitting, and the paperwork the client needs.

blocks.p: A team leader often has several jobs waiting. Put them in order with a simple rule:

head: Priority
Kind of job
Example
rows: A broken handrail at a clinic; a gate hanging off one hinge beside a road
Work with a fixed, close due date
Grills promised for Friday; steel needed by another trade on Monday
Work with a later or no fixed date
Shelving with no date; stock items

blocks.p: Make temporary safety repairs first if a permanent repair will take time, and tell the clients affected if other jobs must move.

sections.title: Planning the method and the sequence

flow: Check and collect the materials against the cut list and the drawing
Mark out and cut; prepare the ends and edges (bevels, root face) as the WPS says
Set out and tack the assembly on a flat bench or jig
Check it: sizes, squareness (diagonals), flatness; correct it while it is only tacked
Weld out in the planned sequence
Clean, grind and inspect the welds and the overall sizes again
Prime and paint (or send for galvanising)
Deliver or fit on site; final inspection; hand over

blocks.p: Each step depends on the one before it. A frame is **tacked and checked before it is fully welded** because mistakes are easy to correct at that stage: a tack can be broken and the part moved. Once the frame is welded out, the same error means cutting welds and starting again.

A rectangular frame is square when its two diagonals are equal. Work out what each diagonal should be with **Pythagoras**: diagonal = √(length² + width²). **Example:** a frame 1,500 mm × 800 mm: √(1,500² + 800²) = √(2,250,000 + 640,000) = √2,890,000 = **1,700 mm**. Measure both diagonals at the tacked stage; if one is longer, ease the frame until they match within the drawing's tolerance, then check again after welding.

Welding heats the steel, which expands and then shrinks as it cools. The shrinking pulls the parts out of line, so a frame can bend, twist or go out of square: **distortion**. A planned order of welding balances the pulls.

ul: Tack every joint first, check the diagonals, and clamp the frame flat to the bench.
Weld opposite corners in turn (for example top left, then bottom right, then top right, then bottom left) rather than going round in order.
Weld one side of each joint, then turn the frame and weld the other side; let joints cool between runs.
On a long joint, use short runs in a planned order (back-step or skip welding) so the heat is spread out.
Pre-set parts slightly against the expected pull where experience shows it helps.
Do not over-weld: a bigger weld than the drawing asks for adds heat and shrinkage.
Check the diagonals during welding and correct any movement early.

head: Point
What it means
Example
rows: Work **stops** at this stage until a named person has checked it and signed
Fit-up of a frame: diagonals checked and signed before any full welding
The client or inspector is invited to watch; if they do not come at the agreed time, work may go on
The client's inspector watching the final dimensional check
A check the team makes and records itself
Leg lengths checked with a fillet gauge after welding

head: Tool
What it shows
Use it for
rows: The steps, who does each, the time, the checks
Every piece to be cut, its size and how many
The steps as boxes joined by arrows, with decision points such as 'Passed inspection?'
Showing the order and what happens when a check fails
Each task as a bar against time, with who does it
Scheduling a team over several days
Items to tick before starting or before leaving for site

blocks.note: Experienced welders still use a pre-start checklist on routine jobs. It is on the jobs you have done a hundred times that it is easiest to skip a step without noticing.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **cut list** lists every piece to be cut for the job: the section, the length, the number needed, and any end preparation.
Work out each length from the drawing. A rail that fits **between** two uprights is the overall width less the two upright widths.

blocks.h: Allowing for saw cuts and stock lengths

blocks.p: Every saw cut turns a strip of steel into swarf: the **kerf**, often about 2 to 3 mm with an abrasive cut-off disc (check your saw). Steel tube, angle and bar usually come in **6 m lengths**. Do not just add up the lengths and divide by 6 m: lay out which pieces come from which length, because a piece cannot be made from two offcuts.
**Worked example:** the 2 stiles and 3 rails above, allowing 3 mm per cut. Total: 2 × 1,800 + 3 × 920 = 6,360 mm, plus 5 cuts × 3 mm = 6,375 mm, so more than one 6 m length is needed.

ul: Add an allowance for waste, mistakes and offcuts that are too short to use, often 5% to 15% depending on the job. **Example:** 25 m of tube needed + 10% = 27.5 m; in 6 m lengths that is 27.5 ÷ 6 = 4.6, so order **5 lengths** (30 m).
To find the percentage extra on an order: (amount ordered − amount needed) ÷ amount needed × 100.
Record useful offcuts so they are used on later jobs.

blocks.p: **Worked example:** a gate has 8 m² to paint, with two coats, and the paint covers about 12 m² per litre per coat. Paint needed = 8 × 2 ÷ 12 = 1.33 L. Allow about 10% for waste and touch-up: about 1.5 L, so buy **2 litres**. Use the coverage on the tin: it varies with the paint and the surface.

List the consumables, because they run out fast and a shortage can stop the job: electrodes or wire, shielding gas, cutting and grinding discs, flap discs, wire brushes, soapstone, primer, paint, thinners, rags, and PPE such as gloves and filter lenses. Estimate from past jobs of a similar size, and check stock before the job starts.

ul: If the WPS calls for **low-hydrogen electrodes**, the plan must include dry storage: a rod oven at the maker's temperature, and taking out only what will be used soon.
Check that gas cylinders hold enough for the job, and order replacements in time.
Check the delivery against the order and the drawing: the section, size and thickness, the length, the quantity.
On a job with a specification, check the labels and the **mill certificate** (the steelmaker's certificate giving the grade and test results), and record the heat number if traceability is required.
Look for damage, bends and heavy rust or pitting. Reject or report anything that does not match before it is cut.

flow: Break the job into steps
Estimate each step from the **actual hours** recorded on similar past jobs
Add up the steps
Add a **contingency** for delays and problems (often about 10% to 15%)
Work out how many days it will take with the people available
Check the order: which steps must wait for others

blocks.p: **Worked example:** a window grill: mark out and cut 2 h, fit and tack 2.5 h, weld 3 h, grind and clean 1.5 h, prime and paint 2 h, fit on site 3 h. Total 14 h. Contingency 10% = 1.4 h, so plan **15.4 h** (15 hours 24 minutes).

ul: **Labour hours** = people × hours each. Two welders working 7 hours each = 14 labour hours.
**Days** = labour hours ÷ (people × productive hours per day). 42 labour hours with 2 people working 7 productive hours a day = 42 ÷ 14 = 3 days.
Productive hours are less than the hours on site: allow for setting up, breaks, travel and cleaning up.

blocks.h: Dependencies, the critical path and float

blocks.p: Some steps cannot start until others finish (welding waits for fit-up; fitting waits for the paint to dry). Others can run **at the same time** (one person cuts the infill bars while another tacks the frame), which finishes the job sooner without rushing any step.

head: Task
Hours
Can start after
rows: Start (it can run while A and C are done)
D Fit infill bars and weld out

blocks.p: The **critical path** is the longest chain of linked tasks: here A, C, D, E, F, G, H. It sets the shortest time the whole job can take, so a delay to any task on it delays the finish. Task B is not on the critical path: it takes 2 hours, but D cannot start until A and C (5 hours) are done, so B has 3 hours of **float** (spare time). B could run up to 3 hours late without delaying the job.

A **milestone** is a key point in the schedule, such as 'all pieces cut', 'frame welded' or 'paint complete'. A **bar (Gantt) chart** shows each task against time, so everyone can see who does what and when.

ul: **Lead time** is the time between ordering an item and its delivery. Order items with long lead times first, and plan work that does not need them in the meantime.
Book shared equipment (the plasma cutter, the crane, the van) early. If another team has it booked, agree a time with them or change the order of your work.
Plan a **back-up** for key resources: a second supplier, a spare machine, another saw, so the work can go on if something fails.
Plan for people: leave, training days, and who can cover a key skill.

blocks.p: **Worked example:** a window grill. Materials: 2 lengths of square tube at J$7,800 = J$15,600; 4 lengths of square bar at J$2,400 = J$9,600; consumables J$3,500; paint J$4,200. Materials total J$32,900. Labour: 15.4 hours at J$1,500 per hour = J$23,100. **Total before GCT: J$56,000.** GCT is then added at the current rate, along with any transport and the shop's overheads and profit as the business sets them.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, in a different order. Keep the figures before GCT separate from the tax, and write 'J$' on every amount.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Planning for safety and site work

blocks.p: Plan safety at the same time as the method, not afterwards. Break the job into its steps first, because each step has its own hazards: cutting, grinding, lifting, welding, painting and fitting at height all need different controls.

ul: Do a **job safety analysis (JSA)** for the steps; choose controls in the right order (eliminate, substitute, engineer, administrate, PPE).
Do as much as possible in the shop, where conditions are controlled, and as little as possible on site or at height.
Plan any **permits**: hot work outside the shop, confined spaces, work on isolated machinery.

**Containers that held fuel or chemicals**, such as a diesel tank that needs a bracket welded on, must be cleaned, tested and declared safe by a competent person, with a permit, before any hot work. Put that in the plan and the timetable.
**Galvanised or coated steel** welded indoors needs fume extraction at the weld in the plan, and a respirator where extraction is not enough.
Plan the PPE, the first aid kit, the extinguisher and the emergency contacts.

blocks.h: Visiting or asking about the site

blocks.p: Before a site job, visit the site or get photos and answers to these questions:

head: Question
Why it matters
rows: How do we get there, and how do we get the steel in?
Transport, a narrow lane or a steep drive, parking, carrying distance, steps
Many welders need a 220 V supply of the right rating; with no suitable supply, plan an engine-driven welder or a generator, with fuel
Who will be there, and when?
Occupants, staff, children, patients or guests: agree working times, barriers and screens
Permits, sign-in, working hours, noise limits, where we can set up
What can burn, and what is overhead or underneath?
Fire risk, overhead lines, buried services, access at height
What is the weather likely to be?
Rain stops site welding and painting; plan cover or another day
Part of the emergency plan for the site

blocks.note: Jamaica's rainy seasons (usually around May to June and September to November) and the hurricane season (1 June to 30 November) affect site welding, painting and deliveries. Plan cover, allow for rain days in the contingency, and secure the site and materials when a storm is forecast.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Taking the right things to site

blocks.p: Load the van from a written checklist: the drawing, the job card, the JSA and permits, the inspection checklist; the tools, the welder, leads and consumables; PPE, screens, the extinguisher, the first aid kit; and fixings and spare parts. A forgotten item can cost a round trip of an hour or more.

flow: Report to the client or the person in charge
Check that the site is safe and as planned: access, power, people nearby, the weather
Set up barriers, screens and the extinguisher; place the generator or engine welder outdoors, with its exhaust away from doors and windows
Brief the team and the client on what will happen and where people must not go
Start work; stop and re-plan if conditions are not as expected

ul: Match tasks to people's skills and experience; give trainees tasks they can do safely, with support and supervision.
Name **one person in charge** on a site job: one person who makes decisions and is the contact for the client and the office.
Say who checks what, and when the hold points are.
Write the roles on the job sheet or a board.

blocks.p: Brief the team before work starts, in a quiet place, with the drawing and the plan in front of you. Go over the aim, the due date and the quality needed; the steps in order; each person's role; the hazards, controls and PPE for each step; and the checks and hold points. Then take questions, and ask each person to say back what they will do first. Invite ideas: the people doing the work often see a better way.

ul: Confirm the planned start and finish dates with the client, so that they can prepare the site and plan around the work.
Tell the client early if a date will change, with the reason and the new date.

blocks.p: Clients change their minds, and drawings have errors. Handle every change the same way:

flow: Write down exactly what is wanted, with a sketch if needed; do not start the change yet
Work out its effect: parts already made, extra material and time, strength and safety, the drawing
Tell the supervisor, who prices it
Get the client's agreement in writing, for example a signed **variation order**, giving the extra cost and the new date
Get the revised drawing; mark the old one **superseded** so no one uses it
Update the cut list, the material order, the schedule and the JSA; brief the team
Record the change in the job file, so the invoice and the inspection match what was agreed

ul: Check progress at set times (for example mid-morning, after lunch and at the end of the day) against the schedule and its milestones.
Record the **actual time** for each step beside the planned time.
Check quality at the hold points as well as speed: rushing to catch up often causes faults and rework.

blocks.p: **Example:** the plan says 20 brackets by Wednesday evening; 15 are done. The team is 5 brackets behind: 5 ÷ 20 = 25% behind the work planned to date. If the whole order is 40 brackets, those 5 are 12.5% of the job.

flow: Find the cause first: a late delivery, a breakdown, more work than expected, a gap in skills, rework
Look at the options: change the order of work, move a person to the slow step, borrow equipment, use the back-up, overtime if allowed, or a new finish date
Never cut out safety controls or quality checks to catch up
Agree the new plan with the supervisor as soon as you know of the delay
Tell the client if the finish date will change
Note the cause, so future plans allow for it

blocks.note: A broken machine need not stop the whole job. Do the work that does not need it (welding parts already cut, preparing the next batch, painting) while the repair or a replacement is arranged.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Before the job card is signed off, inspect the finished work against the drawing and the specification: overall sizes, squareness, weld sizes and quality, the finish. Fix any faults, then record the results on the inspection sheet.

ul: Sort offcuts: keep useful lengths, labelled, for later jobs; put scrap steel in the scrap bin for recycling.
Collect electrode stubs, used discs and wire in metal bins; dispose of paint tins, thinners and rags as their SDSs and local rules say.
Clean, check and return tools and equipment; report anything damaged.
On site, remove barriers and leave the client's premises clean and safe.
The job card signed off, with the actual hours and the materials used.
The inspection sheet with the results.
Any variation orders, NCRs and permits.
Photos of the finished work, if the shop keeps them.

blocks.p: A short **completion report** says: what was done; the checks made and their results; any problems and how they were solved; the planned and actual hours; and **anything still open**, such as a part on back order, with who will follow it up and when. Listing what is still open makes sure it is not forgotten and the client is not let down. The client is shown the work and asked to sign it off.
Hold a short review with the team: what went well, what took longer than planned and why, and what to change next time. Compare the actual hours with the planned hours for each step:

ul: **Overrun** = (actual − planned) ÷ planned × 100. A step planned at 8 hours that took 10 hours overran by 2 ÷ 8 × 100 = 25%.
Record the actual hours and the causes of any overrun, so the next plan and the next quote use real figures.
Fix the cause of any problem for next time: a drawing error, a missing check, a supplier that is always late.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can read a job card, drawing, specification and WPS, and check that the drawing is the latest revision.
I can settle conflicts and unclear points before work starts, and get the answers in writing.
I can put jobs in order of priority, with safety first.
I can put the steps of a fabrication job in a sensible order, and explain why a frame is tacked and checked before welding.
I can plan a welding sequence that limits distortion.
I can explain hold points, witness points and inspection points, and plan them.
I can make a cut list, allow for kerf, and work out the stock lengths needed by laying out each length.
I can work out allowances, paint quantities and consumables, and check materials when they arrive.
I can estimate time with a contingency, and work out labour hours and days.
I can find the critical path and the float in a simple job, and draw a bar chart with milestones.
I can plan for lead times, shared equipment and back-ups.
I can cost a job before GCT, showing materials and labour.
I can plan the safety of shop and site work, including permits and the site visit.
I can give out roles, name one person in charge, brief the team and confirm dates with the client.
I can handle a change through a written variation and a revised drawing.
I can monitor progress, work out how far behind a job is, and re-plan without cutting safety or quality.
I can close out a job: final inspection, clean-up, records, completion report, client sign-off and review.

terms: Contingency
Extra time or money added to a plan in case of problems
Critical path
The longest chain of linked tasks, which sets the shortest time the job can take
Cut list
The list of every piece to be cut, with its size and number
Dependency
A task that cannot start until another has finished
Distortion
Bending or pulling out of line caused by welds shrinking as they cool
Float
Spare time a task has before it delays the whole job
Gantt chart
A bar chart showing each task of a job against time
Hold point
A stage where work stops until a named person has checked and signed
JSA
Job safety analysis: the steps of a job with their hazards and controls
Kerf
The width of material lost in a saw cut
Labour hours
The number of people multiplied by the hours each works
Lead time
The time between ordering an item and its delivery
Milestone
A key point in a schedule, such as 'frame welded'
Mill certificate
The steelmaker's certificate giving the steel's grade and test results
Root gap
The space left between two plates before a butt weld, as the WPS sets it
Routine task
A task done often, with a known method, that still needs planning and checking
Superseded
Replaced by a newer revision and no longer to be used
Variation order
A written record of a change to the job, agreed with the client
Witness point
A stage the client or inspector is invited to watch; work may go on if they do not attend
WPS
Welding procedure specification: the approved method for a weld

c1.title: Shelving racks for a hardware store in Black River
c1.text: Rohan is planning two steel shelving racks for a hardware store in Black River, St Elizabeth. Each rack has 4 uprights of 1,800 mm in 50 × 50 × 5 mm angle, and 8 shelf rails of 1,150 mm in 40 × 40 × 4 mm angle. The 50 mm angle costs J$9,800 per 6 m length and the 40 mm angle J$7,600 per 6 m length. He allows 3 mm for each saw cut. He will also need 2 boxes of electrodes at J$4,200 each. The store wants the racks in 8 working days.

c2.title: A gate and a grill for a house in Yallahs
c2.text: Sanjay and a trainee, Kadeem, will make a driveway gate and a window grill for a house in Yallahs, St Thomas. Sanjay's estimate: cutting 3 h, fitting and tacking 4 h, welding 6 h, grinding and cleaning 3 h, priming and painting 4 h, fitting on site 4 h. The paint must dry overnight before fitting. He adds 15% for delays. Each of them works about 7 productive hours a day. Kadeem will cut the grill's infill bars (2 h) while Sanjay tacks the gate frame (4 h); the grill is tacked after the gate.

c3.title: A ramp handrail at a health centre in Annotto Bay
c3.text: Monique is planning to fit a new steel handrail on the entrance ramp of a health centre in Annotto Bay, St Mary. The rails will be made in the shop and welded on site to the existing posts, which are about 40 years old and rusty at the base. The centre is open from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays, and elderly patients use the ramp. The site is 40 minutes' drive from the shop, and the team will take an engine-driven welder. It is October, and afternoon showers are common.

c4.title: Window grills for apartments in Spanish Town
c4.text: Trevaun's team is making 30 window grills for an apartment block in Spanish Town, St Catherine. The plan says that by the end of day 3, 18 grills should be welded; only 12 are. The cut-off saw broke on day 2 and has not been repaired, although the pieces for 6 more grills were cut before it broke. On day 3 the client phones to ask for a different pattern on the grills not yet made.

c5.title: Closing out a tank stand in Junction
c5.text: Shanoya is closing out a 3 m steel tank stand at a farm near Junction, St Elizabeth. The plan allowed 20 labour hours; the job took 26, mostly because the base plates had to be re-drilled when the drawing showed the holding-down bolts in the wrong place. The overflow-pipe bracket cannot be fitted until a part arrives next week. Offcuts of angle and box section, electrode stubs and empty paint tins are left on site.

questions.q: How many 6 m lengths of 50 mm angle does Rohan need for the 8 uprights?
o: 2 lengths
4 lengths
3 lengths
5 lengths
questions.why: Each 6 m length gives 3 uprights: 3 × 1,800 mm + 3 × 3 mm = 5,409 mm; a fourth would need 7,212 mm. So 8 uprights need 3 lengths (3 + 3 + 2). Dividing 14.4 m by 6 m and rounding down to 2 forgets that pieces cannot be joined from offcuts.

questions.q: What is the cost of the steel and electrodes before GCT?
questions.why: Uprights: 3 lengths × J$9,800 = J$29,400. Rails: each length gives 5 rails (5 × 1,153 = 5,765 mm), so 16 rails need 4 lengths × J$7,600 = J$30,400. Electrodes: 2 × J$4,200 = J$8,400. Total J$68,200; GCT is then added at the current rate.

questions.q: What should Rohan's cut list show for each piece?
o: Only the total length of angle needed for the whole of the job
The price of each piece in J$, so the quote can be built
The section, the length, the number needed and the end cut
The name of the welder who will cut each of the pieces
questions.why: A cut list gives every piece's section, length, quantity and any end preparation, so the right steel is ordered and cut. A total length alone cannot show how the pieces fit into 6 m stock lengths.

questions.q: What total time should Sanjay plan for, including his allowance?
o: 24.0 hours
26.4 hours
28.8 hours
27.6 hours
questions.why: The steps add up to 3 + 4 + 6 + 3 + 4 + 4 = 24 hours. Adding 15% gives 24 × 1.15 = 27.6 hours (27 hours 36 minutes). 26.4 hours would be a 10% allowance and 28.8 hours 20%.

questions.q: Together they work about 14 productive hours a day, yet the job will take more than two working days. Why?
o: Some steps must wait for others, and the paint must dry overnight
A trainee always works at about half the speed of a qualified welder
The 15% allowance has to be doubled when two people share a job
Fitting on site cannot legally be done by a team of two people
questions.why: Dividing hours by people assumes both can work all the time. In practice, welding waits for fit-up, grinding for welding, and fitting for dry paint, so the calendar time is longer than the labour hours suggest.

questions.q: Which two tasks can sensibly be done at the same time?
o: Painting the gate while it is still being welded out by Sanjay
Fitting the gate on site while its paint is drying
Welding the gate out before its frame has been tacked
Kadeem cutting the grill bars while Sanjay tacks the gate
questions.why: Tasks that do not depend on each other can run side by side, which shortens the job without rushing any step. The other pairs break the order of work: each needs the earlier step finished first.

questions.q: If Kadeem's bar cutting takes 3 hours instead of 2, how does it affect the finish?
o: None: the bars have float while the gate is tacked
The whole job finishes 1 hour later than planned
The whole job finishes 3 hours later than planned
The job is late by the 15% allowance on that task
questions.why: The grill is tacked only after the gate frame, which takes Sanjay 4 hours, so the bars have 2 hours of float. A 1-hour overrun uses some of that float and does not touch the critical path.

questions.q: When should Monique plan the site welding?
o: During opening hours, so the staff can keep an eye on it
Outside opening hours, or with another entrance agreed
Whenever the team arrives, to save on travel time
At lunchtime, when fewer patients are using the ramp
questions.why: Elderly patients must not pass arc light, sparks, leads and hot steel, and they still need a way in. Welding when the centre is closed, or closing the ramp with a safe alternative entrance agreed with the centre, protects them.

questions.q: The existing posts are rusty at the base. What should the plan include?
o: Welding to them as they are, since they have lasted 40 years
Painting over the rust so the new rails look neat beside the posts
A check of the posts first, and what to do if they are unsound
Leaving the posts out of the plan, as they are not new work
questions.why: A new rail is only as strong as what it is welded to. The plan should check the posts before fixing, with a contingency (new posts or base plates) if they are weak, so the team is not surprised on the day.

questions.q: The site is 40 minutes' drive from the shop. What is the best way to make sure nothing is left behind?
o: Let each person bring whatever they think they will need
Load the van from a written checklist for the job
Take every tool in the shop, just to be on the safe side
Phone the shop for anything that has been forgotten
questions.why: A written checklist of tools, consumables, PPE, documents and parts is checked off as the van is loaded. A forgotten item means a round trip of over an hour, and taking 'everything' wastes space and time.

questions.q: Afternoon showers are common in October. How should the plan allow for them?
o: Weld through the rain, with a raincoat over the welding PPE
Wait until the dry season to do any of the job at all
Turn up the current so the heat dries the steel as it rains
Weld in the morning, under cover, and stop if it rains
questions.why: Rain on the work, the leads or the welder raises the risk of electric shock and spoils welds and paint. Planning the hot work for the drier morning, with a cover and a rule to stop in rain, keeps both people and quality safe.

questions.q: What should Trevaun do about the client's request for a new pattern?
o: Record and price it, and get it agreed in writing first
Start the new pattern at once, so that no more time is lost
Finish all 30 grills to the old pattern, as first agreed
Make half of the remaining grills in each pattern
questions.why: A change affects cost, time and possibly strength. It is written down, priced, and agreed in writing (for example a signed variation order) before any work on it starts, so both sides know what was agreed.

questions.q: Once the new pattern is agreed, what should happen to the drawing?
o: Keep using the old drawing and tell the welders the change
Ask the welders to remember the new pattern from the phone call
Destroy every copy of the old drawing, including the file copy
Revise it, issue the new one, and mark old copies superseded
questions.why: Everyone must work from one current drawing. Old copies are marked superseded or withdrawn so they cannot be used by mistake, while a file copy is kept as a record of what changed.

questions.q: The saw is still broken. What is the best way to keep the job moving?
o: Stop all work until the saw has been repaired
Cut the steel freehand with a grinder that has had its guard removed
Weld the 6 grills already cut while another saw is arranged
Tell the client the job cannot be finished this month
questions.why: Re-ordering the work keeps people productive: the pieces already cut can be welded while a back-up saw is borrowed or the repair is chased. Removing a guard to save time is never an option.

questions.q: By how much is the team behind the work planned to the end of day 3?
o: About 20%
About 33%
About 40%
About 67%
questions.why: The team is 18 − 12 = 6 grills behind; 6 ÷ 18 × 100 ≈ 33% of the work planned to date. The 20% figure is 6 out of the whole job of 30 grills, which is a different question.

questions.q: By what percentage did the job overrun its planned hours?
o: About 6%
About 23%
About 26%
About 30%
questions.why: Overrun = (26 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 30%. Dividing by the actual hours (6 ÷ 26 ≈ 23%) gives the wrong base: an overrun is measured against the plan.

questions.q: How should the waste on site be handled?
o: Leave it for the farmer, who may find a use for the steel
Keep useful offcuts, recycle scrap, dispose of tins properly
Burn the paint tins and rags in a pile behind the stand
Bury the stubs and short offcuts beside the stand's concrete footings
questions.why: Useful offcuts are kept and labelled for later jobs, scrap steel goes for recycling, stubs go in a metal bin, and paint tins and rags are disposed of as their SDS and local rules say. Burning or burying waste harms people and the land.

questions.q: In the review, what should the team note about the re-drilling?
o: Who drilled the holes, so that person can be blamed
Nothing, since the stand is now finished and paid for
Its cause, so drawings are checked against the site
Only the extra cost, so it can be added to the invoice
questions.why: A review is for learning, not blame. Recording that the drawing did not match the site, and adding a check of bolt positions against the site before drilling, stops the same overrun on the next job.

questions.q: A rectangular frame is 2,400 mm long and 1,000 mm wide. If it is square, what should each diagonal measure?
questions.why: By Pythagoras, the diagonal = √(2,400² + 1,000²) = √6,760,000 = 2,600 mm. Both diagonals should be equal to this, within the drawing's tolerance, before the frame is welded out.

questions.q: The client's inspector asks for a witness point, not a hold point, at fit-up. What does this mean for the plan?
o: Work must stop at fit-up until the inspector has signed
No check of any kind is needed at fit-up on this job
The inspector will do the fit-up instead of the team
He may watch, but work goes on if he does not come
questions.why: At a witness point the inspector is told in advance and may watch, but the work does not have to wait for him. At a hold point, work stops until the named person has checked and signed.
